props.title: Right at Your Door
props.initialSlug: When disaster strikes, there's nowhere to run.

sections.content: Right at Your Door (2006) represents a haunting entry in the post-9/11 disaster thriller genre, taking place in Los Angeles after multiple dirty bombs detonate across the city. Like Cloverfield (2008) and 28 Days Later (2002), it captures the immediate chaos and paranoia of a catastrophic urban event. Director Chris Gorak, previously an art director for Fight Club (1999), brings a claustrophobic intensity by confining much of the action to a single house where Brad (Rory Cochrane) desperately seals himself inside while his wife Lexi (Mary McCormack) remains exposed to the toxic ash outside.

sections.content: The film taps into post-9/11 anxieties about domestic terrorism and environmental catastrophe, similar to Children of Men (2006) and The Road (2009). Its stripped-down approach focuses on moral choices rather than spectacle - should you save yourself or risk death helping others? Contagion (2011) would later explore similar themes of isolation and survival on a larger scale, but Right at Your Door keeps its lens intimate and personal.

The technical execution stands out, particularly in sound design and cinematography. Like War of the Worlds (2005), it creates tension through unseen threats and distant chaos. The toxic ash becomes a character itself, reminiscent of the invisible threat in The Mist (2007). The film's ending delivers a bitter twist that challenges audience expectations, more aligned with darker disaster films like These Final Hours (2013). SUBHEAD: Post-9/11 Disaster Cinema Evolution

sections.content: Right at Your Door marked a shift in disaster films from the grand spectacle of Independence Day (1996) to more grounded, psychological horror. It shares DNA with intimate apocalyptic films like Melancholia (2011) and Perfect Sense (2011), where the focus isn't on saving the world but on human reactions to inevitable doom. The film's exploration of martial law and government response predates similar themes in District 9 (2009) and World War Z (2013).
